citation_title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
supported_use: Progressive resistance training is needed for continued adaptation; intermediate/advanced training uses broader loading and periodized progression
important_limitation: Guidance is broad and older; not a formula for diagnosing an individual's plateau

citation_title: The Effect of Weekly Set Volume on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis
supported_use: Weekly set dose can affect strength gains; medium/high set volumes outperformed low volume in included evidence
important_limitation: Only nine eligible studies; volume needs individual context and more is not automatically better

citation_title: Effect of Resistance Training Frequency on Gains in Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
supported_use: Higher frequency effects appeared primarily driven by additional volume; frequency can distribute volume
important_limitation: Most studies involved untrained participants; frequency alone was unclear when volume was equated

citation_title: Effects of different intensities of resistance training with equated volume load on muscle strength and hypertrophy
supported_use: A range of loads produced adaptations, but heavier conditions produced larger strength increases in this study
important_limitation: Small 12-week study in 30 men with a within-subject design; do not universalize exact percentages

citation_title: Effects of resistance training performed to repetition failure or non-failure on muscular strength and hypertrophy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
supported_use: Training to failure was not required for strength or hypertrophy in the pooled evidence
important_limitation: Included studies were in young adults; subgroup findings do not justify a universal failure rule

citation_title: Effects of Periodization on Strength and Muscle Hypertrophy in Volume-Equated Resistance Training Programs: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
supported_use: Periodized training improved 1RM strength versus non-periodized training when volume was equated; trained participants may benefit from variation
important_limitation: Hypertrophy did not differ; results do not prove one periodization model is best for every trainee

citation_title: Effects of subjective and objective autoregulation methods for intensity and volume on enhancing maximal strength during resistance-training interventions: a systematic review
supported_use: Autoregulation can account for daily fitness fatigue and readiness fluctuations inside a periodized plan
important_limitation: Methods and evidence vary; readiness adjustment is not a substitute for a coherent long-term plan

citation_title: Allostatic Load Measurement: A Systematic Review of Reviews, Database Inventory, and Considerations for Neighborhood Research
supported_use: Terminology boundary: published allostatic-load measurement uses biomarker composites rather than HRV alone
important_limitation: Review context is population and neighborhood research rather than strength coaching; use only to prevent an inaccurate HRV claim

citation_title: Monitoring Athletic Training Status Through Autonomic Heart Rate Regulation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
supported_use: HRV can contribute contextual information but similar changes may accompany positive adaptation and overreaching so other measures are needed
important_limitation: Evidence concerns endurance-trained athletes and does not validate a wearable readiness score for recreational strength trainees

citation_title: Internal and External Training Load: 15 Years On
supported_use: Supports clear distinction between external work and the individual's psychophysiological response
important_limitation: Conceptual framework written for sport performance; it is not a diagnostic formula or direct evidence for a specific plateau intervention
